identification.summary: UNC6293 is the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) designation for a likely Russia state-sponsored cluster that targeted prominent academics and critics of Russia, and later journalists, with patient social-engineering campaigns that tricked victims into creating Google Application Specific Passwords (ASPs) [S1]. GTIG assesses with low confidence that UNC6293 is associated with APT29 / ICECAP [S1].
identification.firstObserved: GTIG observed the activity from at least April 2025 through early June 2025 [S1].
identification.notes: No Microsoft name is known for this cluster; none was found in the sources gathered. Do not merge it with Microsoft's Midnight Blizzard (APT29) tracking; GTIG itself gives only a low-confidence association [S1]. Amazon's August 2025 watering-hole report concerns APT29 and device-code abuse, not UNC6293, and is cited only as context [S5].

attribution.confidence: GTIG: low confidence association with APT29 / ICECAP [S1]. Some secondary coverage states the APT29 link more firmly than GTIG does [S3].
attribution.basis: GTIG assessment from its own observation of the campaigns and shared infrastructure, including a common residential proxy IP across two campaigns [S1]. No government attribution was found in the sources gathered.

objectives: Persistent access to the email accounts of prominent academics and Russia critics, and later journalists, consistent with intelligence collection against Russia-focused individuals [S1]. The stated end goal of the ASP step is persistent mailbox access via a mail client configured with the stolen code [S1].

targeting.notes: GTIG describes targets as prominent academics and critics of Russia, with journalists added in the July 2025 update [S1]. Public reporting says Chatham House Russia expert Keir Giles was targeted in May 2025, with first contact on 22 May 2025 [S2][S3]. Geographic distribution of other victims is not stated in the sources gathered.

capabilities.summary: Low-malware, high-patience social engineering. The actor impersonated the US Department of State, building rapport over several emails and adding spoofed State Department addresses to the cc line; the first email was benign and only asked for a meeting [S1]. After a reply, the target received a benign PDF directing them to create an ASP (named for example 'ms.state.gov') at account.google.com and send the 16-character code to the attacker, who then configured a mail client for persistent access, bypassing multi-factor authentication [S1]. A second campaign used Ukrainian- and Microsoft-themed ASP names [S1]. Per the 10 July 2025 update, the actor re-contacted earlier targets with new look-alike accounts and different ASP names, and separately sent calendar invites with Zoom/Google Meet links plus a Microsoft authentication URL redirecting through the attacker-controlled domain rediruri[.]app, aimed at linking an attacker-controlled device to the victim's Microsoft 365 account (device code flow) [S1]. Victim logins came mainly from residential proxies and VPS servers [S1].

campaigns.name: ASP social-engineering campaign 1 (State Department lure)
campaigns.summary: From at least April through early June 2025 the actor posed as US State Department personnel and used a benign PDF to induce victims to create and share an ASP named 'ms.state.gov' [S1].

campaigns.name: Targeting of Keir Giles
campaigns.summary: Public reporting says Chatham House expert Keir Giles received first contact on 22 May 2025 from a sender using the name 'Claudie S. Weber' with spoofed State Department cc addresses; Google reportedly blocked the attack and disabled the attacker's address [S2][S3].

campaigns.name: ASP campaign 2 (Ukrainian / Microsoft themed)
campaigns.summary: A second campaign used Ukrainian- and Microsoft-themed ASP names; GTIG linked it to campaign 1 through a shared residential proxy IP (91.190.191.117) [S1].

campaigns.name: GTIG publication
campaigns.summary: GTIG published 'What's in an ASP?' disclosing the campaigns and re-securing compromised Gmail accounts; Citizen Lab published related findings [S1][S2].

campaigns.name: Continued operations and device-code variant
campaigns.summary: GTIG saw UNC6293 activity continue in late June 2025, possibly in response to the publication, including re-contact of earlier targets, new accounts with similar usernames, and calendar-invite lures abusing Microsoft device code authentication (update dated 10 July 2025) [S1].

diamond.adversary: Likely Russia state-sponsored cluster tracked by GTIG as UNC6293, low-confidence association with APT29 [S1].
diamond.capability: Rapport-building phishing, State Department impersonation, benign PDF lures, ASP harvesting, and Microsoft device-code/OAuth-style links [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Residential proxies and VPS servers for logins, a shared residential proxy IP across campaigns, throwaway look-alike Gmail accounts, and the redirect domain rediruri[.]app [S1].
diamond.victim: Prominent academics, Russia critics and journalists [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection against individuals who study or criticize Russia, in a period of Russia-Ukraine conflict; the Ukrainian theming of campaign 2 is noted by GTIG without further motive analysis [S1].
diamond.technology: Google ASP feature, which bypasses MFA for legacy mail clients, and Microsoft 365 device code authentication; GTIG says Advanced Protection Program blocks ASP creation [S1].

gaps: Citizen Lab report could not be opened (host unreachable); its facts here come from search-result summaries and secondary coverage [S2][S3]. One search summary gave 14 October 2025 as its publication date while the URL path indicates June 2025; date unverified.
BleepingComputer, SecurityWeek and Risky Bulletin coverage was not opened; only listed in search results.
Number and identity of victims, and whether any compromises succeeded beyond those GTIG re-secured, are not public in the sources gathered.
No Microsoft actor name or MITRE group ID found. Relationship to APT29 / Midnight Blizzard remains a low-confidence GTIG assessment only.
No UNC6293 activity after July 2025 was found in searches.
Full redirect chain and client_id details of the device-code lure were not verified.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is personal and commercial email and identity accounts (Google, Microsoft 365) of Russia-focused experts, including those who advise or brief DoD, rather than government networks. STEP 2: Adversary relies on legitimate authentication features (ASPs, device code) that bypass MFA, so network defenses see only normal logins from residential proxies [S1]. STEP 3: Template is patient rapport-building email with State Department impersonation, then benign PDF, then ASP or device-code grant, then persistent mailbox access [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued low-volume targeting of Russia analysts, academics and journalists using the same pretexts with new accounts and ASP names. MDCOA is applying the pretext to US government or military personnel, using plausible DoS or DoD meeting invitations. Candidate indicators: unexpected ASP-creation notifications, sign-in from residential proxy or VPS addresses, authorization requests to unfamiliar Microsoft applications, links through rediruri[.]app, and first-contact emails with spoofed .gov cc addresses [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track GTIG and Citizen Lab reporting on account-based social engineering of personnel with Russia expertise; personal accounts fall outside DoDIN visibility. (2) Authorities: monitoring personal accounts is limited, so rely on awareness training, voluntary reporting and coordination with providers rather than collection. (3) Mission assurance: enforce hardware-key or Advanced Protection style protection for high-risk staff, disable legacy app passwords and restrict device-code flow where policy allows [S1]. (4) Coordination: route suspected approaches through counterintelligence, the security manager and the provider; share indicators with partners via normal CTI channels.

provenance.importedSummary: UNC6293 is a Russian state-sponsored threat actor identified by Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), which associates them with APT29 with low confidence. They have conducted campaigns utilizing social engineering tactics, including leveraging App-Specific Passwords for account compromises. GTIG has also noted a second campaign by UNC6293 that incorporates Ukrainian themes.
